persons.note: THE 1835 POLL LIST AND A SECOND INDEPENDENT SOURCE. Read from directory_1843, directory_1844, poll_1835. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1a), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. poll_1835 names this person at Chicago by 31 December 1835 and nothing says when they came. THE BOUND FALLS AFTER THE SCENE DATE and the record says so rather than narrowing it: the earliest source that names this person is later than 1 July 1835, so they may have arrived after the day this scene models. present_on_scene_date is `uncertain` for that reason. No figure is drawn (L1). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Curtis, Mrs. James | Letter. | May 4, 1844. | Dismissed.” (second_presb_0529, printed page 183), admitted 1844-05-04 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Curtis' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins J. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a_married_womans_entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Poll list of 1835 — “Curtis, J.” (poll_1835_018, line 303). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Curtis' agrees with the entry's forenames; 2 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

merge_ruling.for_merge: A terminal s, and the initial J agrees with Jacob. Both cards are in the town's records for the scene window: 'Curtis, J.' on the 1835 poll and 'J. Curtiss' in the Democrat of 20 May 1835 (#c009) and 5 August 1835 (#c017).
merge_ruling.against_merge: THE INITIAL J HAS TWO RIVALS ON THE CURTISS SIDE ALONE, AND A THIRD TRADE ON THE CURTIS SIDE. The directories print two J. Curtisses of this town: 'Curtiss, James, State's attorney, 136 Lake' — later the ninth mayor — and 'Curtiss, J. W., gunsmith, res cor North Water and Wolcott', both in Fergus 1843 and again in Norris 1844. An initial that could expand to two full forenames in the cluster attaches to neither: R2, the rule the newspapers' identity.json ratified. And Jacob S. Curtis is a third man with a third trade — 'Curtis, Jacob S., water borer, bds Michael McDonald' in Fergus 1843, 'res M. McDonald's' in Norris 1844 — so the fold would have to pick one of two Curtisses and then overwrite a printed occupation. Refused by a ratified rule; no ballot needed.
